> **JohnFP:** Holography was so much simpler when I wasn't looking for micro answers to questions. Just expose a plate, develop it and yell WOW! It seems the more I learn the more questions I have, but I love it!Like what happens to the AmDi when light hits it? Ok, somehow we get a Cr+++ Ion. Is it the Cr+++ ion that is used for crosslinking the gelatin? What happens to the NH4? Is it reduced to N2 and H2O? Is NH4 were the Cr gets the additional electrons? Is the NH4 that crosslinks the gelatin. This is proving to be difficult information to find.

Taking Michaels suggestion I started a new thread. Here is what I found out, probably known to some/most.

> **http://www.geocities.com/Heartland/Flats/7439/thesis09.htm:** When a gelatin film, sensitized with ammonium dichromate (intrinsic sensitivity in the blue/green region), is exposed to actinic radiation, the hexavalent chromium ion Cr6+ is photoinduced [B.9] to trivalent Cr3+ either directlyCr2O2- + 14H+ + 6e --> 2Cr3+ + 7H2Oor indirectlyCr2O2- + H2O + 2H+ --> H2CrO42H2CrO4 + 6 H+ + 3e --> 2Cr3+ + 5H2O + 3OThe trivalent chromium forms cross-link bonds between carboxylate groups of gelatin chains. This cross-link differentially hardens the gelatin of the exposed and relatively unexposed regions. The hardness differential form the latent image.
 

Had to try that. Anyway this answers some fundimental questions but still not how the actinic reation (defintion of actinic - Chemically reactive rays of the electromagnetic spectrum) alters the AmDi on a micro level. It does state it is the Cr+++ that is used in the crosslinking. But again more questions. Where does the hexavalent CR ion come from. Is that formed when the AmDi is disolved in water?

If you continue reading it states that the dark reaction is when CR+6 changes to the CR+3, I guess without actinic radiation as is references shelf life. But it does not state why.

Peace!

posts.content_md:
[quote:80a475cc68]But I have some doubts that the Cr3+ is responsible for the latent image although this is mentioned in literature again and again since about 1850(?).[/quote:80a475cc68]

What doubts and why?

Actually the presentation given M. Boulte also stated that it's not directly due to Cr3+. The Cr3+ seems to be the final stage of a long, involved process that seemed to involve some forms of chemical "resonances". That is, a whole series of extremely short lived intermediate compounds. It seems that non-actinic ionisations to these "resonances" don't go as fast as actinic ones which apparently accounts for the slow rate of dark reaction.

I've actually had doubts about the Standard Model of scattering. It seems that conditions for Rayleigh scattering are not met by a fairly dense large collection of molecules. It works in some biological molecules (eye color, for instance) because of the long-chain chromatophore backbone on the protein molecule, but as far as I'm aware, gelatin has no such backbone.

posts.content_md:
Hi!

> **Dinesh:** What doubts and why?

Years ago I produced Ronchi rulings for optical testing. 

I used the DCG process suggested by Vasco Ronchi in an article in Applied Optics for this purpose to make a contact copy of a master Ronchi ruling. 

I also looked for some literature about DCG in Gmelin's handbook

and all articles (even the first in Justus von Liebigs Annals published

about 1850-1870) gave this mechanism that Cr3+ would harden

the exposed parts of the gelatin.

As a first test I tried a photo negative of a 

page of a book that contains a coarse "raster". 

After processing the grating I checked the result under a

stereo microscope. I was very surprised that apparently

the parts that were exposed to light dissolved in water.

I could distinguish it because the text and drawings on

that page were copied on the DCG layer, too.

This would be quite logical since the products of the redox

reaction are easy to dissolve in water.

I recently checked the old grating and the negative 

(I already posted this finding on the old forum) and I am pretty 

sure that the exposed DCG dissolves and it isn't hardened. 

Therefore it cannot be hardened by Cr3+. Unfortunately I

had no time to try a new check. But I believe the first

article (as far as I remember by von Liebig himself?) might have been 

wrong.

I believe the first scientists who used DCG didn't have microscopes

of a high quality. Besides it is quite a physiological problem to decide if a crater is embossed oder recessed. Years ago I read an article in

Sky&Telescope magazine about this effect and lunar observers

and the analysis of Lunar orbiter imagery.

Liebig might have taken an recessed part of the gelatin for an

embossed area by mistake. 

I am still not 100% sure if this is correct or if I am wrong 

because even new papers published

in 2001 give the same information and even books about printing

or etching techniques based on DCG give them. But I will check

this aspect as soon as possible when I take a new DCG hologram.

> Actually the presentation given M. Boulte also stated that it's not directly due to Cr3+. The Cr3+ seems to be the final stage of a long, involved process that seemed to involve some forms of chemical "resonances". That is, a whole series of extremely short lived intermediate compounds.

Yes, of course all complex redox reactions require such short

lived intermediates.

> I've actually had doubts about the Standard Model of scattering. It seems that conditions for Rayleigh scattering are not met by a fairly dense large collection of molecules. It works in some biological molecules (eye color, for instance) because of the long-chain chromatophore backbone on the protein molecule, but as far as I'm aware, gelatin has no such backbone.

In my opinion a DCG hologram behaves exactly like a phase

grating (with a modulation of the index of refraction).

posts.content_md:
[quote:5390e4fa97]I've actually had doubts about the Standard Model of scattering. It seems that conditions for Rayleigh scattering are not met by a fairly dense large collection of molecules. .

Why? Due the molecular "density" on the media or due the large molecular size that could absorb light at various parts?

[/quote:5390e4fa97]

Well, both. The model for Rayleigh scattering is basically that the scattering center is a dipole. Also, the dipoles themselves need to be well seperated so that there is not the usual phase combinations in dense media causing forward propagation. Any driven oscillator at high frequencies oscillates at pi out of phase with the driving force. The blue of the sky will only be true at rare matter densities. Lower down in the atmosphere, the density of molecules is too thick for Rayleigh. However, Einstein and Smoluchowski (independantly) determined that the reason for blue skies lower down in the atmosphere was due to random statistical variations that caused random rarefication and so caused Rayleigh scattering. In gelatin, you have giant molecules in close quarters so that any dipoles, if they exist, will have many complex phase inter-relationships between each other. It's difficult to see how the w^4 relationship requirement of Rayleigh scattering can predominate. Due to the large size of the gelatin molecule I would rather expect Mie scattering. The fact that scattering in DCG seems predominantly white seems to strengthen this.

[quote:5390e4fa97]I was very surprised that apparently the parts that were exposed to light dissolved in water. [/quote:5390e4fa97]

So the DCG acted like a negative resist? (Have I got this right? A negative resist is the one that causes the exposed parts to soften?) Anyway, I was wondering if perhaps bulk DCG acted in a different way to a thin-film surface DCG. The holographic properties of bulk DCG, as in a volume hologram, are supposedly due to either bubbles or cracks in the gelatin structure at locally hardened sites (depending on which theory you believe) made more pronounced by alcohol as Sergio stated. In a thin layer neither of these effects would occur. However the modulation is of the order of perhaps 10^(-3) or 10^(-2), may even be lower . Is it possible then that the greater solubility of the exposed, apparently "hardened", DCG is due to processes other than just density, since the difference in density is so low? Charge density reacting with the polar water, perhaps?

If the completely unhardened gelatin, with no dichromate, would be expected to show gelatin in the processing solutions, then surely a better figure of merit of hardening would be the ratio of gelatin solution in a rocessing solution from a dichroamted system to gelatin in the same processing solution, at the same temperature with no dichromate. Have any experiments been conducted to determine such a ratio? Also, why is there an assumption that dissolution rate depends only on hardening (presumably density). If two different substances were equally dissolved in water, does not the dissolution rate depend on the structure and bonds within the two substances? In fact, the presence of dissolved gelatin in the processing solutions seems to be the cause of the consternation. However, the processing solutions is mainly alcohol. What is the process that governs diossolution in a type B solvent? Is it purely density?

"Why should there not be dissolved gelatin in the processing solution?"

If "integrity" of the layer (e.g. layer thickness) is paramount for volume processes, we may care about how much bulk gelatin is lost on processing. General wisdom on

dichromated processes suggested a crosslinking/hardening/tanning action on colloids like

gelatin. So if Cr "hardening" additionally implied solution (at least of small

quantities of gelatin), there would be something wrong with that theory (I wouldn't be surprised though).

"Is it that "hardened" gelatin cannot dissolve?"

It depends on the extent it has been hardened/crosslinked/tanned previously. The more

it's hardened, the higher the water temperature (and, incidentally, the higher the pH) it will resist to.

Or, in other words: the more the gelatin has been hardened, the less it will be

swelled by water.

"... then surely the rate of dissolution from "hardened" gelatin must depend

on the level of hardening?"

Yes but there might be yet additional factors to play a role:

bloom strength and the gel's individual history (the mechanical strength of a gel might greatly differ if

you applied a 1% gelatin solution or some 20%).

"Have any experiments been conducted to determine such a ratio?"

Not to my knowledge.

"In fact, the presence of dissolved gelatin in the processing solutions

seems to be the cause of the consternation."

Yes, indeed.

"However, the processing solutions is mainly alcohol."

...and (warm) water - prior to the alcohol baths...

[quote:6c4431b375]Do you think spending less time in the fixer for older plates and perhaps a bit longer swelling bath, will compensate for some of the natural hardining in geriatric plates.[/quote:6c4431b375]

To an extent. As the plates get older, I fix for less. After about two weeks, I barely fix at all. Just a quick dunk in and out. This only works so far, though. After about three weeks even zero fixing causes dim green images. It's possible that warming the water as well as decreasing fixing might work. However, Martin's reply to me made me think that I've never warmed the water. I knew one person in a previous lab who consistently did, but he never seemed to get good results with warm water. Now, with this thread, I'm wondering whether the warmed water lost more gelatin mass.

The problem is that there are so few papers on DCG out there. It seems that not a lot of work is being done on it.

[quote:6c4431b375="Colin Kaminski"][quote:6c4431b375]The holographic properties of bulk DCG, as in a volume hologram, are supposedly due to either bubbles... [/quote:6c4431b375]

Could this be the source of the Rayleigh scattering?[/quote:6c4431b375]

I don't think so. Rayleigh scattering specifically implies a forth power law. As you know, the amplitude of a forced oscillation is:

A = (F/m)/((w_0^2 - w_d^2)^2 + gamma^2*w_d^2)^0.5

where w_0 is the natural frequency

w_d is the driving frequency

gamma is the resistance or drag.

In optics, the E field of the incoming light causes the positive-negative centers in a simple atomic system to oscillate and so form an oscillating dipole. The oscillating, charged dipole then sends off em waves of it's own due to it's oscillations, these waves having an amplitude dependant on the amplitude of the dipole. If you apply the above equation to a dipole, you replace F by the Coulomb force due to charge seperation in the dipole and the w_d is the frequency of the incoming wave. You now get the amplitude of the scattered wave due to the dipole and you can see that there is an inverse w_d^4 dependance. In the above equation there is (( w_0^2 - w_d^2)^0.5) in the denominator but the intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude so the intensity of the dipole radiation is inversely dependant on (w_o^2-w_d^2)^2 or, if w_d, the incoming frequency of light, is very high, on w_d^4. Since lambda is inversely proportional to w, the amplitude of the scattered radiation is much greater in the blue end since the ratios of scattering for red and blue will now be:

I_blue/I_red = (w_red)^4/(w_blue)^4 = ( lambda_blue)^4/(lambda_red)^4

which is huge. 

A bubble is not a dipole so it should not have this w_d^4 behaviour. Also, the above analysis depends on the fact that the scattered radiation is truly scattered. If the matter density is high, this scattered radiation will soon drive other nearby dipoles. Since there is a pi phase shift between driving frequency and driven frequency, you soon cancel out the two, interferometrically. Mie scattering also behaves like this for small particles but red-shifts and eventually white shifts as the particles ("bubble") size increases, so it's possible that the bubbles are a source of Mie scattering.
